city_center.name: Tularosa village + Highway 54/70 pistachio corridor
city_center.landmark: Tularosa Basin high-desert plain at ~4,400 ft between the Sacramento Mountains and White Sands; pistachio groves line Highway 54/70 toward Alamogordo
city_center.notes: the basin takes its name from the red reeds ('tularosa') that grew near local springs; elevation, dry air and alkaline soil suit pistachio trees. PistachioLand and Eagle Ranch (Heart of the Desert) are the landmark groves. sources: homestratosphere.com Tularosa Basin pistachio towns; newmexico.org Alamogordo; farmprogress.com.

cultural_notes: the Tularosa Basin is named for the red reeds ('tularosa') that once grew near local springs; it is an arid high-desert zone at roughly 4,400 ft whose dry air and alkaline soil suit pistachio trees (source: homestratosphere.com Tularosa Basin pistachio towns; farmprogress.com Eagle Ranch)

the basin has the climate for pistachios, pecans and grapes, with numerous nut farms and wineries between Alamogordo and Tularosa -- PistachioLand and Eagle Ranch / Heart of the Desert are the two largest pistachio groves (source: newmexico.org Alamogordo; rvingwithrex.com; nationalnutgrower.com Heart of the Desert)

Eagle Ranch (Heart of the Desert) began in the early 1970s when the Schweer family planted pistachios in the New Mexico high desert -- a documented family-farm origin, not a fabricated claim (source: nationalnutgrower.com; stephwaxpoetic.com)

Tularosa village retains a historic Hispano acequia-and-cottonwood character; White Sands National Park lies just west (INFERRED cultural framing from region + basin geography -- verify tone before production)
